title: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play
hook: the string too tight snaps, too loose won't play

segments.voice: Yesterday: equanimity, upekkha, the rock in the eight winds. Your line was let it be as it is. Did you take a breath before reacting? Day twenty.
screen: `EQUANIMITY — LET IT BE AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: There's a young monk named Sona, and he is trying so hard. He's been practicing walking meditation, the kind you learned about a few days ago, so intensely and for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path he walks is stained with it. And he's getting nowhere. Sitting alone, he starts to think about quitting. Going home. Using his family's money to do some good in the world instead. The Buddha hears about it and comes to see him. And he doesn't say try harder. He doesn't say give up. He asks about music.
screen: `SONA TRIES SO HARD.` → `HIS FEET ARE BLEEDING.` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS ABOUT MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Before he was a monk, Sona was skilled at the lute, a stringed instrument. So the Buddha asks him: when the strings were too tight, did the lute play well? No. When the strings were too loose, did it play well? No. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned just right? Then it played beautifully. It's the same with effort, the Buddha says. Too much, and you become restless and strained. Too little, and you become lazy. Find the right tuning. Sona takes the advice, and the story says that before long, he reaches awakening. This is the middle way, and it's where the Buddha's whole teaching began. Remember the first sermon, in the deer park? Before he taught the four truths, he told his five companions there are two extremes to avoid. On one side, chasing pleasure: the life he'd had in the palace. On the other, punishing the body: the years he'd spent nearly starving himself as a seeker. Both, he said, lead nowhere good. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is the eightfold path you already know. So the middle way isn't a bland compromise, halfway between two things. It's more like tuning. A string that's in tune isn't half-tight. It's exactly right for that string, that instrument, that day. And it needs retuning, again and again, because strings drift. Some days you need more effort. Some days you need rest. The skill isn't finding the answer once. It's listening, and adjusting.
screen: `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE, TUNED.` · `EFFORT, THE SAME WAY.` · `TWO EXTREMES TO AVOID.` · `NOT HALFWAY. TUNED.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE WAY.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about seventy-five seconds. Sit, and check your tuning. Is your body too tight? Clenched jaw, raised shoulders, gripping hands? Let a little go. Is it too loose? Slumped, drowsy, drifting? Lift the chest a little and brighten your attention. Look for the place in between: upright and relaxed, awake and easy. When you drift one way or the other, gently retune. The bell holds the time.
The middle way. Between indulgence and self-punishment, not a compromise but a tuning, adjusted again and again. Twentieth word.
Your line: tune. Today, notice one thing you're doing too hard, or too little. Adjust it by one notch, and see how it plays. Day twenty.

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the middle way as the path between sensual indulgence and self-mortification, and apply it to everyday practice, balancing effort and ease in meditation, eating, sleep and work.

myth: the middle way means a bland compromise
it's like tuning a string: exactly right, and retuned as it drifts.
the Buddha taught the middle way in his first sermon
two extremes to avoid, then the path between them.
the Buddha told Sona to try harder
he asked about the lute: too tight won't play either.

fork.setup: you're Sona. your feet are bleeding from practice and you're thinking of quitting. the Buddha comes to you. what does he do?
options: tells you to push through the pain.
asks how a lute plays when its strings are too tight.
fork.reveal: he asks about the lute. too tight, too loose: neither plays. effort needs tuning too, and Sona, the story says, soon awakens.

original.note: Pali: the middle way. majjhima, middle; paṭipadā, path, way of practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't do anything too much.
what it means: the path between chasing pleasure and punishing the body, found by tuning, again and again.
what a scholar hears: majjhimā paṭipadā, named in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11) as the eightfold path; the lute simile is in the Sona Sutta (AN 6.55).

sources.ref: Sona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 6.55); also Vinaya, Mahavagga V
Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11): the two extremes

notes: Sona Kolivisa story paraphrased from AN 6.55 (bleeding feet on the walking path, thought of returning to lay life and making merit with his wealth, the lute simile, later arahantship). Confirm details.
The instrument is a vina, rendered 'lute'. Confirm.
Two extremes from SN 56.11 paraphrased: confirm.
